title: Is There a Rising Triple
statement: Return `true` if there are three positions `i < j < k` (not necessarily next to each other) with `numbers[i] < numbers[j] < numbers[k]`, otherwise `false`. The inequalities must be strict.

hints.nudge: You only need to remember two things while scanning: the smallest number so far, and the smallest 'second number' of a rising pair so far. Why is that enough?
hints.pattern: Keep `first` (smallest value seen) and `second` (smallest value that has a smaller value before it); the first number bigger than `second` completes a triple.
hints.pseudocode:
first = second = infinity
for x in numbers:
  if x <= first: first = x
  elif x <= second: second = x
  else: return true
return false
hints.walkthrough: Checking all triples is O(n^3), and checking each middle element against the best left and right neighbours is O(n) extra memory. A single pass works with two variables. `first` is the smallest number so far. `second` is the smallest number so far that has something smaller before it, i.e. the best end of a rising pair. A new number x that is not larger than `first` becomes the new `first` (it starts a better pair later). Otherwise, if x is not larger than `second`, it gives a rising pair with a smaller end: it becomes the new `second`. Otherwise x is larger than a number that is larger than something earlier: a rising triple exists. Note that `first` may be updated after `second` was set; this is fine because `second` still proves that a pair exists before it.
